Isabel Rios

life-007 · development · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like numbers more when they are about something somebody actually needs to decide. Playing with an orchestra feels different: I do not need it to solve anything for me to want to be there.

  • family: Lives with her mother and older brother; father lives in another state.
  • finances: Mother’s fluctuating cleaning contracts mean careful monthly budgeting.
  • geography: El Paso, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: Spanish and English; family travels locally to see relatives when schedules allow.
  • school: Public high school with dual-credit courses and a small orchestra.
  • accessOpportunities: Public library, school instruments, and a teacher-supported college visit.
  • Age 4–5

    In 2014, Isabel arranged stones into pretend shops outside her apartment. She liked calculating exchanges with invented money and became frustrated when her brother changed the prices halfway through the game without telling her.

  • Age 6–7

    At six, she began translating simple school notices with her mother, while adults handled legal and medical matters. In 2017, a librarian introduced her to wordless picture books that she repeatedly borrowed for their visual jokes.

  • Age 8–9

    In 2018, Isabel chose the viola because the school had one available. She disliked practicing scales alone but loved the moment an ensemble chord became balanced, and she gradually learned to hear her part inside it.

  • Age 10–11

    During 2020, her mother’s work hours became uncertain. Isabel used library hotspot loans for school and made a color-coded shopping list to help stretch groceries, without losing her taste for elaborate imaginary restaurant menus.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve, she tried a coding club and found debugging oddly satisfying. In 2023, she left after its meeting time conflicted with orchestra, keeping a small number-guessing game on her computer that she occasionally improved.

  • Age 14–15

    In 2024 and 2025, Isabel helped her brother compare used-car costs and worked several school concession shifts. She discovered that explaining numbers calmly was harder when the purchase mattered personally than when it was homework.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen in 2026, she is exploring dual-credit mathematics and a summer ensemble in West Texas. She hopes to visit a campus but is uncertain whether her interest in calculations depends on having a clear real-world question.

Life now

  • enjoys: Ensemble playing · Debugging small programs · Comparing prices
  • avoids: Solo auditions · Pressure to translate beyond her knowledge
  • activities: Orchestra · Dual-credit preparation · Concession shifts
  • demonstratedSkills: Builds clear comparison sheets · Hears ensemble balance · Patient error checking
  • unfamiliarActivities: Large laboratories · Living outside El Paso
  • motivations: Making choices less confusing · Belonging in a group
  • ambitions: Keep music in her life · Try a course with unfamiliar classmates · She imagines a secure adult routine with family visits, shared music, and room in the budget for an occasional unfamiliar experience.
  • struggles: Solo practice motivation · Worries about spending on optional activities
  • supports: Mother · Brother · Orchestra teacher · Librarian
  • practicalConstraints: Program fees · Limited evening transport · Shared computer

Still uncertain: Would she enjoy abstract mathematics with no immediate application? · How much would she miss ensemble life away from home?
